title: Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11)
hookLine: the king sees, takes, and arranges a loyal husband's death

lines: WHEN KINGS GO OUT TO BATTLE.
A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.
cards: At the turn of the year, the text says, the time when kings go out to battle, David sends his general Joab, his servants and the whole army. And David stays in Jerusalem.
That one detail sits at the start of the chapter like a stone in a shoe: the king isn't where kings go. One evening he gets up from his bed and walks on the roof of the king's house.
From the roof he sees a woman washing herself, and she is very beautiful. He doesn't look away. He sends someone to find out who she is.

teach.h: HE SEES. HE SENDS. HE TAKES.
teach.b: The answer comes back: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite, who is away fighting in David's own army. Listen to the verbs, all of them the king's. He sees.
He sends. He takes. The text gives Bathsheba almost no words; the few she sends are a message: I am with child.
He calls Uriah home from the front: go down to your house. Uriah sleeps at the palace door with the servants instead.
The ark and Israel and Judah are in tents, he says, and Joab is camped in the open field; how could I go home, eat and drink, and lie with my wife? David gets him drunk. He still won't go home.
So David writes Joab a letter and sends it with Uriah himself: put him at the front of the hardest fighting, then pull back, so he's struck down. Uriah carries his own death in his hand. It happens.
David's reply to Joab sounds almost calm: don't let this thing be evil in your eyes; the sword devours one as well as another. Bathsheba mourns her husband, and then David brings her into his house.
And the narrator, silent about right and wrong all chapter, speaks once: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." In Hebrew it's an echo. Let it not be evil in your eyes, says David.
It was evil in the eyes of the Lord, says the narrator. The king could see a woman on a roof.
He couldn't see what he was doing.

how: Jews read the story of David and Bathsheba in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the next chapter, the prophet Nathan's rebuke, is read as part of the same story.

games.q: you're Uriah, called home from the front by the king. he tells you to go down to your house. what do you do?
o: go home to your wife, as the king says.
sleep at the palace door with the servants.
ask the king why he really called you.
games.why: he sleeps at the palace door: the ark and the army are in tents, so how could he go home? even drunk, he won't go.

practice: Power turns up in ordinary places: over a child, an employee, a waiter, someone who owes you. Let one of those places come to mind and ask, quietly, what your power lets you not notice about this person, because you don't have to.
Don't punish yourself; just name one thing, and if you pray, you can hold it before God.

wordCard.voice: Bathsheba. The woman the king saw, sent for and took, while her loyal husband slept at the palace door. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah, in 2 Samuel 11:3.

carryVoice: Your line: power can blind. The narrator sees what the king won't see. Until tomorrow.
